body.p: William Radcliffe was a prominent local resident who lived in Bouverie Street, Carlton, and worked as a partner in a company of wholesale merchants, McClure, Valantine and Company, based in a’Beckett Street in the city.

Radcliffe was a Sergeant in the North Melbourne Rifle Brigade in 1860 when it was split in two, with the two parts becoming the Metropolitan Corps and the Carlton Corps. He was then elected to head the latter and was accordingly promoted to the rank of Captain. By the time he resigned he held the rank of Major. In August 1860, a notice announcing the first meeting of the newly formed Carlton Volunteer Rifle Company placed in The Argus newspaper was signed ‘William Radcliffe, Senior Sergeant, North Melbourne Company’. One month later a meeting of the Carlton Rifles was held at the University Hotel in Lygon Street to elect their officers and commanding officer. Senior Sergeant Radcliffe was unanimously appointed to command the Company, and hence became Captain Radcliffe of the Carlton Volunteer Rifle Company.

Radcliffe was a keen cricketer and in 1860 the same year that the Carlton Rifles was founded, and he became the founding President of the Carlton Cricket Club. He may have also been associated with the formation of the Carlton Football Club in the 1860s. He and the Carlton Rifles appear to have maintained a connection with the Carlton Football Club. An 1872 programme for the football club’s ‘Athletic Sports, to be held on the Carlton Cricket Ground’ says that the ‘Band of the Carlton Rifles will be present. By kind permission of Major Radcliffe’.
In October 1864 the members of the Carlton Rifle Company presented Radcliffe with a handsome sword in appreciation of his services to the corps. A newspaper account at the time noted that:

Everyone acquainted with the history of the volunteer movement here will be aware that for a long time Captain Radcliffe had an up-hill task, and that much merit and much courage was required to win for him and for his corps the present high position they occupy. The entire force will be pleased to hear of the honour done to an able officer, a splendid rifleman, and a right good volunteer. (The Australasian, 22 October 1864)

In his private life he lived with his wife and children at Bainbridge Terrace in Bouverie Street, Carlton, just south of Grattan Street. In December 1875, as he was winding up his affairs in preparation for leaving the colony for New Zealand, two significant things happened to his family. In early December his daughter was married - in a ceremony that took place in the family home in Bouverie Street. Later that month, just before Christmas, his four-year-old son died. In early 1876 the family departed, sailing to Christchurch on the South Island. It was here that four years later, in March 1879, William Radcliffe died aged only 48.
